question: What happens to the amount of energy transferred from one step to the next in a food chain?

supplied_evidence.text:
Reflection of light at curved surfaces211 Our EnvironmentGovernment’s Gift for Students’ Progress
The biomass in a trophic level may be more or less than the other
trophic levels. Biomass is a measure of the amount of food available. When
animals eat, only a small proportion of their food is converted into new
tissue, which inturn forms the food for the next trophic level. Part of
biomass that animals eat is used to provide energy needed for staying alive,
rest passes out of its body.
The biomass pyramid shows that animals are relatively inefficient in
converting food into body tissues, the remaining part of the food being
undigested is passed out as waste, or broken down in respiration to supply
energy for activities such as feeding. Many animals convert not more than
10% of their food into their body tissues, in some herbivores, it is even
less. Let us take an example of a food chain which has been worked out in
some detail- one in which we are involved when we eat fish. In this chain
the phytoplankton on the surface water of sea are food producers. They
trap energy from sunlight. The zooplankton feed on the microscopic plants
and the fish in turn feed on the zooplankton; we are at the end of the chain
when we eat the fish.

Food is the source of energy for organisms
that are used in the growth and rebuilding the
parts of the body; that are constantly wearing out.
The food by its nature is the chemical energy

Photosynthesis is an essential process for the life. The energy in
sunlight, carbon dioxide and the water which are needed by all living things
belong to nonliving things. As a result of photosynthesis, these can be
made available in a suitable form of energy the food to the world of living
things the animals or consumers, only by the green plants the producers.
The food chains and food webs help in the transfer of the food and energy
from the producers to different consumers.

Animals obtain the minerals from the plant or animal food or both.
Thus the mineral matter is constantly being removed from the earth to
become a part of the plant, which may become a part of animal body.
Try to identify the basic sources of various foods we eat. For example
curd that we eat is processed from milk, which comes from a cow, which
in turn eats grass. The grass carries out photosynthesis and prepares food.
In every case, the origin of food materials can be traced back to green
plants.
Once the food is eaten, its energy follows a variety of pattern through
the organisms. Not all the food can be fully digested and assimilated. Hair,
feathers, insect exoskeletons, cartilage and bone in animal foods, cellulose
and lignin in plant foods cannot be digested by the most animals. These
materials are either ejected by defecation or regurgitated as indigested
remains.
Assimilated energy (that is not lost through respiration or excretion)
is available for the synthesis of new biomass through growth and
reproduction. Organisms lose some biomass by death, disease or annual
leaf-drop, where they enter the detritus pathways of the food chain i.e.,
after the death and decomposition of organisms the materials flow back
into the environment(soil, water, air). The remaining biomass is eventually
consumed by herbivores or predators and its energy there by enters the
next higher trophic level in the ecosystem.
The materials keep on cycling i.e. entering the living beings and through
death and decay returning to the soil and atmosphere Such a flow of
materials between organisms and their environment is called Cycling of
materials or mineral circulation or Biogeochemical cycles (You have
learnt in class IX ).
Energy enters the producers in the ecosystem from the sun in
the form of solar energy or solar radiation. No other organisms
except green plants and Photosynthetic bacteria due to due to the
presence of chlorophyll are capable of absorbing solar energy and
converting it into chemical energy (food).

parsed_output.answer: In a food chain, the amount of energy transferred from one step to the next decreases. This is because only a small proportion of the energy from one trophic level is passed on to the next. For example, when animals eat, only a small part of their food is converted into new tissue, which forms the food for the next trophic level. The rest of the energy is used for the animal's life processes, such as staying alive, or is lost as heat or waste. Typically, only about 10% of the energy from one level is transferred to the next, with the majority being lost as heat or through metabolic processes.
